move.title: Grind the masala, poach in coconut
move.body: Goan fish curry (xitt kodi) is the everyday meal of India's west coast: white fish poached in a sour, red coconut curry. Its flavor comes from a masala you grind yourself: toasted coriander, cumin, peppercorns, and dried red chiles blended with coconut milk, garlic, ginger, and tamarind. You'll toast and grind the paste, cook it out, and poach the fish in it at a bare simmer, with basmati rice.

why.title: Toast whole spices
why.body: Whole seeds toasted in a dry pan release oils that ground spices have already lost. Pull them when they smell strong and darken one shade; a minute more and they turn bitter.

why.title: Cook the paste out
why.body: Raw ground spices taste dusty. Frying the paste in oil until it darkens and the oil separates cooks them through.

why.title: Tamarind for sourness
why.body: Goan curries balance rich coconut with sour tamarind. Add it in stages and taste; brands vary a lot in strength.

why.title: Poach, don't boil
why.body: Fish in a curry is poached: the sauce at a bare simmer, the fish added last and cooked only until it flakes, to 145°F.

wrong.fix: Start the toasting over. Burnt seeds make the whole curry bitter.

wrong.sign: The coconut milk split and looks oily
wrong.fix: It boiled hard. It still tastes right; keep it below a simmer once the fish is in.
Add a pinch of sugar and a splash more coconut milk.
It was stirred. Shake the pan instead, and cut thicker pieces.

quiz.q: Why toast whole spices before grinding?
choices: They release fresh oils and deepen in flavor
quiz.explain: A minute, until they smell strong.

quiz.q: What temperature does the fish reach?

steps.text: Rinse the basmati until the water runs clear. Cook it with its water and salt: boil, cover, lowest heat 15 minutes, then rest off the heat.
Toast the coriander, cumin, peppercorns, and chiles in the dry skillet over medium heat, shaking the pan, until fragrant and a shade darker.
Blend the toasted spices, turmeric, garlic, ginger, and the masala's can of coconut milk to a smooth paste.
steps.look: Brick red and smooth, with no whole seeds.

steps.text: Slice the onion thin and slit the jalapeño lengthwise. Heat the oil in the skillet and soften the onion over medium heat.
Add the paste and the jalapeño. Fry, stirring, until it darkens and oil pools at the edges.
steps.look: Darker red, with oil separating at the edges.

steps.text: Add the curry's coconut milk, 1 tablespoon of the tamarind, and the salt. Bring to a bare simmer. Taste and add tamarind to balance.
Pat the fish dry and lay it in the sauce in one layer. Spoon sauce over it.
Wash your hands and the board.
Cover and keep at a bare simmer, shaking the pan rather than stirring.
Scatter the cilantro and serve over the rice.
steps.look: Opaque fish in a glossy red-orange sauce.
